Judge the ASSERTIONS, not the titles. A test whose name mentions the same words

Traps specific to this project:

- **Boundary requirements need the exact boundary value.** A requirement about age exactly 65 is NOT covered by a case passing 64 or 66, or by a case asserting a senior fare for age 70. Only an assertion whose input is literally the boundary value, and whose expected value is the adult fare, would fail if the comparison operator were wrong. Nearby ages exercise the sides, not the edge.
- **Omission requirements need an assertion of absence or of exact shape.** A requirement that some element must appear in output is not covered by a test that only checks the first element, the length in a way that passes either way, or a `toContain`/`toMatchObject` partial match that stays true when the element is dropped. An exact `toEqual` on the whole collection, or an explicit assertion on the last element, does fail when the item is omitted; a spot-check of the middle does not.
- **vitest specifics.** An `it.skip`, `it.todo`, `describe.skip`, or a commented-out block does not run, so it cannot fail and cannot cover anything. An `it` whose body contains no `expect` — or only `expect` calls inside an untaken branch — also cannot fail. A `.only` elsewhere in the file does not change whether a given case exercises the requirement; judge the case itself.
- **TypeScript reading.** Values may come from fixtures, factory helpers, or constants defined at the top of the file rather than inline in the case. Trace them: an assertion using a named constant may well pin the boundary or the exact expected output. Conversely, a snapshot assertion (`toMatchSnapshot`) with no inline snapshot in the file gives you no evidence about the asserted values — treat it as not demonstrating coverage.
